summary: Krypton sputtering enables body-centered cubic tantalum film deposition on silicon at temperatures as low as 200 °C, compared to 350–650 °C for argon, while achieving higher electronic conductivity consistent with clean-limit superconductivity. Coplanar waveguide resonators exhibit median quality factors of 4.1 million at single-photon power (350 °C Kr), and transmon qubits with 20 µm capacitor gaps reach median $Q_1$ up to 14 million.
motivation: Scalable manufacturing of superconducting qubits requires back-end-of-line compatibility with the 400 °C temperature ceiling used in semiconductor foundries, but conventional argon sputtering of α-Ta demands substrate temperatures exceeding 400 °C, creating a bottleneck for industrial translation of high-performance Ta-based devices.
method: Magnetron sputtering with krypton instead of argon gas was used to deposit 100 nm α-Ta films on Si(100) at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 600 °C. Electronic transport, X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and cryogenic microwave measurements characterized the films; coplanar waveguide resonators and transmon qubits with Manhattan-style junctions were fabricated to benchmark device performance.
result: Kr-deposited films show residual resistivity ratio ~30 (versus ~15 for Ar at comparable T), mean free paths exceeding the Ginzburg-Landau coherence length ($\ell_{5\,\mathrm{K}} \gtrsim \xi_{\mathrm{GL}}$), reduced Ta/Si intermixing at the interface, and no detectable Kr impurities by secondary ion mass spectrometry; 350 °C Kr resonators achieve $\delta_\mathrm{LP} = 2.45 \times 10^{-7}$ and transmons without oxygen descum reach $Q_1 = 14.4 \times 10^6$ with $T_1 \approx 0.71$ ms.
